messages.subject: Simulating loss
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luis,

I would like to calculate the loss of genetic diversity in simulated scenarios. In particular, I would like to calculate the difference in allelic richness, number of rare and common alleles, fixed loci for a decreasing number of individuals. Would you be able to suggest me suitable functions in dartR or other tools/software?

Thank you,
Manuela

- For a tutorial of RDA see: https://popgen.nescent.org/2018-03-27_RDA_GEA.html

Cheers,
Luis

messages.subject: Re: Simulating loss
messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuela,

In your previous email, you said:

I should give more background. I am working on two rare species affected by the 2019 "Black fire" season.
I have not done any simulation yet, but I was considering calculating how much genetic diversity would be lost in the event of a new fire.
So I would like to calculate how much genetic diversity (allelic richness, rare alleles, number of fixed alleles) is lost if 5 trees die, or 10, or 15, or 20 ecc...
I can probably keep it very simple and just remove a progressively higher number of individuals from my dataset and see how the diversity metrics change. But I was wondering if there was a more sophisticated way to do it.
Also, if the fire removes individuals, hence a number of alleles, then Ne would be reduced for a bit and that should cause further loss by drift. I as wondering if you know a way to infer loss by drift as well.

You could try the simulations in dartR in which real datasets can be used as input (see code below). You can read our simulations tutorial here: Simulations tutorial · green-striped-gecko/dartR Wiki (github.com) <https://github.com/green-striped-gecko/dartR/wiki/Simulations-tutorial>
I am also attaching the input files for the simulations using the code below and a plot with the final results of the simulations.
To use the code below, you should install the developing version of dartR (first three lines of the code below).

Cheers,
Luis

## installing developing version of dartR
# library(devtools)
# install_github("green-striped-gecko/dartR@devluis")
library(dartR)
library(hierfstat)
library(reshape2)
library(patchwork)
# this is a real dataset
t1 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
# filtering by missing data
t1 <- gl.filter.callrate(t1, threshold = 1)
# assigning dummy chromosome and position to SNP's
t1$chromosome <- as.factor(rep("1", nLoc(t1)))
t1$position <- 1:nLoc(t1)
####################################################
##### first comparing simulations vs real dataset
####################################################
# Creating the reference table for running gl.sim.WF.run
sim_table <- gl.sim.WF.table(file_var = "ref_variables.csv",
                             x = t1,
                             interactive_vars = FALSE)
# running the actual simulations
# the C++ code of the function is compiled the first time
# the function is run so it takes a bit
res_sim_test <- gl.sim.WF.run(
  file_var = "sim_variables.csv",
  ref_table = sim_table,
  x = t1,
  number_iterations = 1,
  every_gen = 10,
  sample_percent = 100,
  real_pop_size = TRUE,
  # running just the first phase
  store_phase1 = FALSE,
  interactive_vars = FALSE,
  gen_number_phase2 = 100,
  phase1 = FALSE
)
# Subsetting the first iteration of the simulations
all_gen <- res_sim_test$iteration_1
# subsetting the first generation
first_gen <- all_gen$generation_1
# using PCA to compare real vs simulated data
# real dataset
pca_real <- gl.pcoa(t1, plot.out = FALSE)
gl.pcoa.plot(pca_real, x = t1)
# simulated data
pca_sim <- gl.pcoa(first_gen, plot.out = FALSE)
gl.pcoa.plot(pca_sim, x = first_gen)
# comparing heterozygosity
gl.report.heterozygosity(t1)
gl.report.heterozygosity(first_gen)
#PCA across generations animation
pca_gen <- lapply(all_gen, gl.pcoa, plot.out = FALSE)
gl.pcoa.plot(pca_gen, all_gen)
# Comparing simulations against theoretical expectations
pop_sizes_test <- as.numeric(table(pop(t1)))
res_diags <- gl.diagnostics.sim(res_sim_test,
                                Ne = pop_sizes_test[1],
                                pop_he = 1)
####################################################
##### simulating a bottleneck based on a real dataset
#####################################################
# table of populations
table(pop(t1))
# dropping smallest population (Ne for this population is Infinite)
t1 <- gl.drop.pop(t1, pop.list = "SEVERN_BELOW")
# Calculating effective population size
# download Neestimator2 executable from link below and move it to your working
# directory (see function documentation)
# (http://www.molecularfisherieslaboratory.com.au/neestimator-software/)
res_NE <- gl.LDNe(t1)
# getting estimates
pop_sizes <- lapply(res_NE, "[", 6, 2)
pop_sizes <- as.numeric(unlist(pop_sizes))
# population size of each population in the simulations (must be even, space
# delimited and in quotes)
# pop sizes phase 1
pop_size_phase_1 <- pop_sizes
pop_size_phase_1 <- round(pop_size_phase_1)
# converting odd population sizes to even
pop_size_phase_1 <- (pop_size_phase_1 %% 2 != 0) + pop_size_phase_1
pop_size_phase_1 <-
  paste(as.character(pop_size_phase_1), collapse = " ")

# simulating bottleneck (reduction in popsize)
###### Simulation parameters ######
bottleneck_sizes <- c(0.5, 0.7, 0.9)
# Generation interval at which simulations should be stored
gen_interval <- 10
# generations phase 1
gen_phase1 <- 50
# generations phase 2
gen_phase2 <- 50
# dataframe to store values
plot_fin <- data.frame(
  gen_vec = NA,
  variable = NA,
  value = NA,
  stat = NA,
  bottleneck = NA
)
###### loop across different bottleneck sizes ######
for (i in bottleneck_sizes) {
  # pop sizes phase 2
  pop_size_phase_2 <- (1 - i) * pop_sizes
  pop_size_phase_2 <- round(pop_size_phase_2)
  # converting odd population sizes to even
  pop_size_phase_2 <- (pop_size_phase_2 %% 2 != 0) + pop_size_phase_2
  pop_size_phase_2 <-
    paste(as.character(pop_size_phase_2), collapse = " ")
  # total generations
  gen_total <- gen_phase1 + gen_phase2
  # running the actual simulations
  res_sim <- gl.sim.WF.run(
    file_var = "sim_variables.csv",
    ref_table = sim_table,
    x = t1,
    number_iterations = 1,
    every_gen = gen_interval,
    sample_percent = 100,
    store_phase1 = TRUE,
    interactive_vars = FALSE,
    phase1 = TRUE,
    real_pop_size = FALSE,
    number_pops_phase1 = 2,
    population_size_phase1 = pop_size_phase_1,
    # generations before the bottleneck
    gen_number_phase1 = gen_phase1,
    number_pops_phase2 = 2,
    # generations after bottleneck
    gen_number_phase2 = gen_phase2,
    population_size_phase2 = pop_size_phase_2
  )
  # Subsetting the first iteration of the simulations
  all_gen_bottle <- res_sim$iteration_1
  # generations vector
  gen_vec <- seq(0, gen_total, gen_interval)
  # calculating allelic richness
  res_ar <- lapply(all_gen_bottle, function(x) {
    tmp <- genind2hierfstat(gl2gi(x))
    tmp_res <- round(colMeans(allelic.richness(tmp)$Ar,
                              na.rm = TRUE), 3)
    return(tmp_res)
  })
  #formatting data
  res_ar <- Reduce(rbind, res_ar)
  res_ar <- as.data.frame(cbind(res_ar, gen_vec))
  res_ar_plot <- melt(res_ar, id = "gen_vec")
  res_ar_plot$stat <- "Allelic Richness"
  # calculating heterozygosity
  res_het <- lapply(all_gen_bottle,
                    gl.report.heterozygosity,
                    plot.display = FALSE)
  #getting polymorphic loci
  res_poly <- lapply(res_het, "[", , "polyLoc")
  res_poly <- as.data.frame(Reduce(rbind, res_poly))
  res_poly <- t(apply(res_poly, 1, "/", unlist(res_poly[1,]))) * 100
  res_poly <- as.data.frame(cbind(res_poly, gen_vec))
  colnames(res_poly) <- c(popNames(t1), "gen_vec")
  res_poly_plot <- melt(res_poly, id = "gen_vec")
  res_poly_plot$stat <- "Loss of polymorphic loci (%)"
  # getting heterozygosity
  res_hetero <- lapply(res_het, "[", , "uHe")
  res_hetero <- as.data.frame(Reduce(rbind, res_hetero))
  res_hetero <- cbind(res_hetero, gen_vec)
  colnames(res_hetero) <- c(popNames(t1), "gen_vec")
  res_hetero_plot <- melt(res_hetero, id = "gen_vec")
  res_hetero_plot$stat <- "Heterozygosity"
  # storing values for each bottleneck
  plot_tmp <- rbind(res_ar_plot, res_poly_plot, res_hetero_plot)
  plot_tmp$variable <- as.character(plot_tmp$variable)
  plot_tmp$bottleneck <- paste0("Bottleneck ", as.character(i * 100), "%")
  plot_fin <- rbind(plot_fin, plot_tmp)
}
# format data for plotting
#removing first row with NAs
plot_fin <- plot_fin[-1, ]
plot_fin$stat <- as.factor(plot_fin$stat)
plot_fin2 <- split(plot_fin, f = plot_fin$stat)
# plotting
p <- lapply(plot_fin2, function(x) {
  ggplot(x, aes(x = gen_vec, y = value, color = variable)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = gen_phase1, color = 'blue') +
    annotate(
      x = gen_phase1,
      y = Inf,
      label = paste0("Bottleneck"),
      vjust = 2,
      geom = "label"
    ) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(stat ~ bottleneck,
               scales = "fixed",
               ncol = 1) +
    labs(x = "Generations",
         y = "",
         col = "Populations") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
})
# plotting using package patchwork
p2 <- p[[1]] + p[[2]] + p[[3]]
# printing plot
print(p2)
# saving plot
ggsave(
  filename = paste0("sim_bottleneck.pdf"),
  width = 12,
  height = 8,
  units = "in",
  dpi = "retina",
  bg = "transparent"
)

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to use the argument 'as.pop=' to display various features on my PCoA plot, e.g. discrete phenotypes or population groupings based on geography. In most cases these alternative population datasets contain missing data, which I have coded as 'NA' in the metadata file.

When these are plotted using gl.pcoa.plot() the 'NA' values appear gray, which is good; however, the problem is that the NA values are plotted on top of everything else. For example, I plotted observations of flavor onto my original PCoA using gl.pcoa.plot(x_pca, x, as.pop="flavor", xaxis=1, yaxis=2). The attached screenshot shows a portion of the resulting plot.

Based on the placement of the label it is possible to infer where the "bitter" flavors are clustering, yet the majority of observations are hidden behind the gray 'NA' points. Is there a way to plot the actual data on top of the NA points, or to increase the opacity of the 'NA' points (alpha=0.5?) so that the actual data can still be viewed?

Thanks,
David

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuela,

There are some simple simulation functions in dartR.

For example the gl.sim.ind function allows to “create” a specified number of individuals based on the frequencies of a genlight object, so you could simply use that one.

e.g.

gl <- gl0 #initial population

for (i in 1:20) gl <- gl.sim.ind(gl, 50)    #sample/create 50 individuals based on allele frequencies

gl.report.heterozygosity(gl0)

gl.report.heterozygosity(gl)

runs for 20 generation simply resampling 50 individuals (so this is a drift only model)

to add mutation during the 20 runs:

gl <- gl0 #initial population

for (i in 1:20) {

gl <- gl.sim.ind(gl, 50)

gl <- gl.sim.mutate(gl, 1e-8)  #mutation rate 1e-8

}

A bit more sophisticated is the function

gl.sim.offspring(father, mothers) os here you can simulate offsprings (from defined pairs, in case of wright fisher you simply have the same fathers and mothers and the offspring per mother is one.

Here you can then for example specify a number of generations you want to have between the events you are interested and rerun the function accordingly.

If you do not want to have a simple drift only scenario you could then also use gl.sim.mutate (which adds mutation to a genlight object).

Using those building blocks it is fairly straight forward to create simple simulation, or you use the more sophisticated tool Luis described, which allows more fine tuning in terms of parameters, linkage between loci etc.

If all of this is not good you may want to have a look at slimR (which integrates nicely with Slim and dartR).  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1755-0998.13916?af=R

Here you have a full flexibility in terms of simulations, but at the cost you need to learn how to set up models in slim(R).

Cheers, Bernd

Hi Manuela,

In your previous email, you said:

I should give more background. I am working on two rare species affected by the 2019 "Black fire" season.
I have not done any simulation yet, but I was considering calculating how much genetic diversity would be lost in the event of a new fire.
So I would like to calculate how much genetic diversity (allelic richness, rare alleles, number of fixed alleles) is lost if 5 trees die, or 10, or 15, or 20 ecc...
I can probably keep it very simple and just remove a progressively higher number of individuals from my dataset and see how the diversity metrics change. But I was wondering if there was a more sophisticated way to do it.
Also, if the fire removes individuals, hence a number of alleles, then Ne would be reduced for a bit and that should cause further loss by drift. I as wondering if you know a way to infer loss by drift as well.

You could try the simulations in dartR in which real datasets can be used as input (see code below). You can read our simulations tutorial here: Simulations tutorial · green-striped-gecko/dartR Wiki (github.com) <https://github.com/green-striped-gecko/dartR/wiki/Simulations-tutorial>

I am also attaching the input files for the simulations using the code below and a plot with the final results of the simulations.

To use the code below, you should install the developing version of dartR (first three lines of the code below).

Cheers,
Luis

## installing developing version of dartR
# library(devtools)
# install_github("green-striped-gecko/dartR@devluis")
library(dartR)
library(hierfstat)
library(reshape2)
library(patchwork)
# this is a real dataset
t1 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
# filtering by missing data
t1 <- gl.filter.callrate(t1, threshold = 1)
# assigning dummy chromosome and position to SNP's
t1$chromosome <- as.factor(rep("1", nLoc(t1)))
t1$position <- 1:nLoc(t1)
####################################################
##### first comparing simulations vs real dataset
####################################################
# Creating the reference table for running gl.sim.WF.run
sim_table <- gl.sim.WF.table(file_var = "ref_variables.csv",
                             x = t1,
                             interactive_vars = FALSE)
# running the actual simulations
# the C++ code of the function is compiled the first time
# the function is run so it takes a bit
res_sim_test <- gl.sim.WF.run(
  file_var = "sim_variables.csv",
  ref_table = sim_table,
  x = t1,
  number_iterations = 1,
  every_gen = 10,
  sample_percent = 100,
  real_pop_size = TRUE,
  # running just the first phase
  store_phase1 = FALSE,
  interactive_vars = FALSE,
  gen_number_phase2 = 100,
  phase1 = FALSE
)
# Subsetting the first iteration of the simulations
all_gen <- res_sim_test$iteration_1
# subsetting the first generation
first_gen <- all_gen$generation_1
# using PCA to compare real vs simulated data
# real dataset
pca_real <- gl.pcoa(t1, plot.out = FALSE)
gl.pcoa.plot(pca_real, x = t1)
# simulated data
pca_sim <- gl.pcoa(first_gen, plot.out = FALSE)
gl.pcoa.plot(pca_sim, x = first_gen)
# comparing heterozygosity
gl.report.heterozygosity(t1)
gl.report.heterozygosity(first_gen)
#PCA across generations animation
pca_gen <- lapply(all_gen, gl.pcoa, plot.out = FALSE)
gl.pcoa.plot(pca_gen, all_gen)
# Comparing simulations against theoretical expectations
pop_sizes_test <- as.numeric(table(pop(t1)))
res_diags <- gl.diagnostics.sim(res_sim_test,
                                Ne = pop_sizes_test[1],
                                pop_he = 1)
####################################################
##### simulating a bottleneck based on a real dataset
#####################################################
# table of populations
table(pop(t1))
# dropping smallest population (Ne for this population is Infinite)
t1 <- gl.drop.pop(t1, pop.list = "SEVERN_BELOW")
# Calculating effective population size
# download Neestimator2 executable from link below and move it to your working
# directory (see function documentation)
# (http://www.molecularfisherieslaboratory.com.au/neestimator-software/)
res_NE <- gl.LDNe(t1)
# getting estimates
pop_sizes <- lapply(res_NE, "[", 6, 2)
pop_sizes <- as.numeric(unlist(pop_sizes))
# population size of each population in the simulations (must be even, space
# delimited and in quotes)
# pop sizes phase 1
pop_size_phase_1 <- pop_sizes
pop_size_phase_1 <- round(pop_size_phase_1)
# converting odd population sizes to even
pop_size_phase_1 <- (pop_size_phase_1 %% 2 != 0) + pop_size_phase_1
pop_size_phase_1 <-
  paste(as.character(pop_size_phase_1), collapse = " ")

# simulating bottleneck (reduction in popsize)
###### Simulation parameters ######
bottleneck_sizes <- c(0.5, 0.7, 0.9)
# Generation interval at which simulations should be stored
gen_interval <- 10
# generations phase 1
gen_phase1 <- 50
# generations phase 2
gen_phase2 <- 50
# dataframe to store values
plot_fin <- data.frame(
  gen_vec = NA,
  variable = NA,
  value = NA,
  stat = NA,
  bottleneck = NA
)
###### loop across different bottleneck sizes ######
for (i in bottleneck_sizes) {
  # pop sizes phase 2
  pop_size_phase_2 <- (1 - i) * pop_sizes
  pop_size_phase_2 <- round(pop_size_phase_2)
  # converting odd population sizes to even
  pop_size_phase_2 <- (pop_size_phase_2 %% 2 != 0) + pop_size_phase_2
  pop_size_phase_2 <-
    paste(as.character(pop_size_phase_2), collapse = " ")
  # total generations
  gen_total <- gen_phase1 + gen_phase2
  # running the actual simulations
  res_sim <- gl.sim.WF.run(
    file_var = "sim_variables.csv",
    ref_table = sim_table,
    x = t1,
    number_iterations = 1,
    every_gen = gen_interval,
    sample_percent = 100,
    store_phase1 = TRUE,
    interactive_vars = FALSE,
    phase1 = TRUE,
    real_pop_size = FALSE,
    number_pops_phase1 = 2,
    population_size_phase1 = pop_size_phase_1,
    # generations before the bottleneck
    gen_number_phase1 = gen_phase1,
    number_pops_phase2 = 2,
    # generations after bottleneck
    gen_number_phase2 = gen_phase2,
    population_size_phase2 = pop_size_phase_2
  )
  # Subsetting the first iteration of the simulations
  all_gen_bottle <- res_sim$iteration_1
  # generations vector
  gen_vec <- seq(0, gen_total, gen_interval)
  # calculating allelic richness
  res_ar <- lapply(all_gen_bottle, function(x) {
    tmp <- genind2hierfstat(gl2gi(x))
    tmp_res <- round(colMeans(allelic.richness(tmp)$Ar,
                              na.rm = TRUE), 3)
    return(tmp_res)
  })
  #formatting data
  res_ar <- Reduce(rbind, res_ar)
  res_ar <- as.data.frame(cbind(res_ar, gen_vec))
  res_ar_plot <- melt(res_ar, id = "gen_vec")
  res_ar_plot$stat <- "Allelic Richness"
  # calculating heterozygosity
  res_het <- lapply(all_gen_bottle,
                    gl.report.heterozygosity,
                    plot.display = FALSE)
  #getting polymorphic loci
  res_poly <- lapply(res_het, "[", , "polyLoc")
  res_poly <- as.data.frame(Reduce(rbind, res_poly))
  res_poly <- t(apply(res_poly, 1, "/", unlist(res_poly[1,]))) * 100
  res_poly <- as.data.frame(cbind(res_poly, gen_vec))
  colnames(res_poly) <- c(popNames(t1), "gen_vec")
  res_poly_plot <- melt(res_poly, id = "gen_vec")
  res_poly_plot$stat <- "Loss of polymorphic loci (%)"
  # getting heterozygosity
  res_hetero <- lapply(res_het, "[", , "uHe")
  res_hetero <- as.data.frame(Reduce(rbind, res_hetero))
  res_hetero <- cbind(res_hetero, gen_vec)
  colnames(res_hetero) <- c(popNames(t1), "gen_vec")
  res_hetero_plot <- melt(res_hetero, id = "gen_vec")
  res_hetero_plot$stat <- "Heterozygosity"
  # storing values for each bottleneck
  plot_tmp <- rbind(res_ar_plot, res_poly_plot, res_hetero_plot)
  plot_tmp$variable <- as.character(plot_tmp$variable)
  plot_tmp$bottleneck <- paste0("Bottleneck ", as.character(i * 100), "%")
  plot_fin <- rbind(plot_fin, plot_tmp)
}
# format data for plotting
#removing first row with NAs
plot_fin <- plot_fin[-1, ]
plot_fin$stat <- as.factor(plot_fin$stat)
plot_fin2 <- split(plot_fin, f = plot_fin$stat)
# plotting
p <- lapply(plot_fin2, function(x) {
  ggplot(x, aes(x = gen_vec, y = value, color = variable)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = gen_phase1, color = 'blue') +
    annotate(
      x = gen_phase1,
      y = Inf,
      label = paste0("Bottleneck"),
      vjust = 2,
      geom = "label"
    ) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(stat ~ bottleneck,
               scales = "fixed",
               ncol = 1) +
    labs(x = "Generations",
         y = "",
         col = "Populations") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
})
# plotting using package patchwork
p2 <- p[[1]] + p[[2]] + p[[3]]
# printing plot
print(p2)
# saving plot
ggsave(
  filename = paste0("sim_bottleneck.pdf"),
  width = 12,
  height = 8,
  units = "in",
  dpi = "retina",
  bg = "transparent"
)

messages.body_plain:
G'day David

 From your emails it is not clear why you are including individuals
listed as NA, because they have missing data in a pcoa plot.   PCoA does
not like missing data as it fills in missing values with the overall
average for the dataset.  You should be removing individuals with excess
missing data.

PCoA is usually done in a step wise manner, going from the broader
scales to finer scales to reveal patterns in your data.  First step
might be your ingroup, or a specific clade (based on a phylogeny), then
you remove the most obvious outliers and run it again until you get to a
point where it's no longer informative for the populations included.

If you are trying to compare different portions of your dataset then you
need to exclude those individuals that you aren't trying to compare.
This can be done using an index command.  The ! means does not, if you
wanted to only select a certain population or combination of populations
then change the ! to =

index <- gl@other$ind.metrics$pop !="NA"
gl <- gl[ index, ]

This example includes only two pops and removes all others.

index <- gl@other$ind.metrics$pop =="pop_name1" |
gl@other$ind.metrics$pop =="pop_name2"
gl <- gl[ index, ]

Alternatively you can use the following commands to do a similar thing.

gl <- gl.drop.pop(gl, pop.list=c('pop_name1'))
gl <- gl.drop.pop(gl, pop.list=c('pop_name1','pop_name2'))

You can substitute drop for keep too.

Cheers
Peter

Hi Kimani,

I guess that you are using the function gl2genalex to export a genlight object to genalex format.

The issue might be due to the following:

In the CRAN version of dartR (i.e.install.packages('dartR')), the individuals are exported in the same order as in the genlight object. However, Genalex requires that individuals be ordered by population. This issue has been fixed in the developing of version of dartR (i.e. devtools::install_github('green-striped-gecko/dartR@dev').

You could also use the function gl.impute for imputing missing data. We recommend filtering on missing data (i.e. gl.filter.callrate) using a threshold of at least 0.5 before imputation. Also, it is important to read the function documentation of gl.impute and consider what the consequences of imputation would be in downstream analyses, taking into account that imputation is not 100% accurate.

Cheers,
Luis

  theme_bw()+

David

alpha_val <- 0.05

#Change theme, add transparency to NA points, modify legend NA point, add legend title

res + geom_point(color = "white")+
  theme_bw()+

  geom_point(alpha = ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(res$data$pop), alpha_val,1))+
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(unique(res$data$pop, fromLast = T)), 21, 19))))+
  labs(color = "Flavor")

Best,
David

messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

Background:
I haven't found the answer to my question in this forum, so here goes. My goal is to develop a SNP genotyping assay for an individual (fish, in this case) that yields data within a five day window. I have a DArTseq dataset, and all analyses indicate that the sample set is comprised of three distinct species, with varying degrees of anthropogenic introgression. This is a sportfish that has been moved around for decades.

In order to conserve native stocks/populations, agencies need to receive genotyping data within a 10-14 day window, which is too short for DArT. Instead, I am attempting to develop a TaqMan assay using loci that represent fixed differences among the three species. I have followed the tutorial/vignette, but I haven't found a function that provides a list of loci that represent fixed differences among populations.

Question 1:
Is there a function that converts a fd object back into a gl object? (from here, I can run loc.names function).

Question 2:
Is there a work-around that extracts names of loci/sequence tags representing fixed differences within a fd object?

Thanks for the continued support!
Mike Sandel
